euronews.description: A video widely shared on social media appears to show a handheld device intercepting a drone. lemonde.description: Ce premier paiement de 3,2 milliards d’euros, destiné à aider le gouvernement ukrainien à boucler son budget, sera suivi, « dans les prochains jours », d’un deuxième de 6 milliards d’euros pour financer l’achat de drones, a précisé la présidente de la Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.

france24fr.title: Canicule : plus de dix heures d'attente pour les passagers d'un Eurostar
france24fr.description: Des centaines de passagers ont dû patienter plus de dix heures après l'immobilisation d'un train Eurostar sous une chaleur écrasante. Parti de Paris, le train s'est arrêté près de Compiègne à la suite d'une alerte incendie. Les voyageurs racontent cette longue attente dans des conditions particulièrement difficiles.

france24fr.title: 🔴 Séismes au Venezuela en direct : au moins 164 morts et 1000 blessés, selon Delcy Rodríguez
Emmanuel Macron reçoit la Première ministre italienne pour mettre en scène leur "bonne entente"
france24fr.description: Emmanuel Macron reçoit la Première ministre italienne Giorgia Meloni à Antibes pour le premier sommet bilatéral franco-italien depuis son arrivée au pouvoir en 2022. Après plusieurs années de tensions, les deux dirigeants veulent relancer leur coopération sur des dossiers stratégiques comme la défense, l'énergie, le spatial et les grands enjeux européens.

france24fr.title: Tunisie : huit ans de prison pour la militante anti-raciste Saadia Mosbah
france24fr.description: En Tunisie, la peine de prison de la militante antiraciste Saadia Mosbah a été confirmée en appel mardi 23 juin, selon ses avocats. Fondatrice de l’association Mnemty, engagée dans la lutte contre les discriminations raciales, elle avait été arrêtée le 6 mai 2024 et poursuivie, avec d’autres membres de l’organisation, pour des accusations de malversations financières. Les précisions de notre correspondante Lilia Blaise.

france24fr.title: Manifestations au Kenya : deux ans après, la peur d'un nouveau drame
france24fr.description: Au Kenya, ce 25 juin marque le deuxième anniversaire des manifestations contre la loi de finances de 2024, dont la répression avait fait plus de 60 morts et des centaines de blessés. Alors que la société civile appelle à de nouveaux rassemblements, beaucoup redoutent une réponse musclée des autorités dans un contexte de violences policières récurrentes.

france24fr.title: Au Gabon, les partis politiques sommés de se mettre en conformité
france24fr.description: Au Gabon, le gouvernement lance un ultimatum aux partis politiques. Les autorités demandent aux 104 formations recensées de se conformer aux nouvelles exigences administratives et légales sous peine de sanctions. Une démarche que certains opposants considèrent déjà comme une atteinte au pluralisme démocratique.

france24fr.title: Au Zimbabwe, une réforme ouvre la voie au maintien de Mnangagwa jusqu'en 2030
france24fr.description: Au Zimbabwe, le Sénat a approuvé un projet de réforme constitutionnelle prévoyant notamment le passage du mandat présidentiel de cinq à sept ans. Cette modification permettrait au président Emmerson Mnangagwa de rester au pouvoir jusqu'en 2030 sans organiser de nouvelle élection présidentielle.

france24fr.title: Au Bénin, les jeux vidéo au service de la mémoire et du patrimoine
france24fr.description: Comment transmettre l’histoire aux jeunes générations à l’ère du tout-numérique ? Au Bénin, des créateurs développent des jeux et expériences interactives pour faire découvrir le patrimoine autrement. Cartes à collectionner, réalité augmentée et univers inspirés du jeu vidéo servent de nouveaux outils de transmission culturelle.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 : les immigrés redoutent l'ICE, un supporter expulsé témoigne
france24fr.description: Aux États-Unis, un père de trois enfants arrêté par l’ICE lors d’un match de football l’été dernier met aujourd’hui en garde les supporters immigrés contre les risques qu’ils prennent en assistant aux matchs de la Coupe du Monde de football. Jessica Le Masurier, Yves Schaeffner et Sarah Andersen vous présentent cette enquête exclusive. Nous préservons l’anonymat de cette famille pour des raisons de sécurité.

france24fr.title: Devoir de vigilance : TotalEnergies face à une décision de justice historique sur le climat
france24fr.description: Le tribunal judiciaire de Paris rend ce jeudi sa décision dans le procès intenté contre TotalEnergies par plusieurs ONG et la Ville de Paris. Au-delà du cas du géant pétrolier, le jugement pourrait redéfinir la responsabilité climatique des grandes entreprises françaises.

france24fr.title: Donald Trump lance les festivités des 250 ans des États-Unis en célébrant son propre bilan
france24fr.description: Pour ouvrir les célébrations des 250 ans de l’indépendance américaine, Donald Trump a surtout mis en avant son action et critiqué ses prédécesseurs, brouillant la frontière entre commémoration et meeting politique. Malgré son optimisme sur l’Iran et l’état du pays, les sondages montrent une opinion publique largement sceptique sur sa politique.

france24fr.title: La canicule se poursuit en France, le record de la nuit la plus chaude une nouvelle fois battu
france24fr.description: Plus de 50 millions d'habitants en vigilance rouge. La canicule se poursuit sur la France, qui vit jeudi une nouvelle journée suffocante, avant un début d'amélioration attendu en soirée, du moins sur la façade atlantique. Le record de la nuit la plus chaude jamais enregistrée en France a une nouvelle fois été battu dans la nuit de mercredi à jeudi.

france24fr.title: Ukraine : Zelensky absent de la conférence sur la reconstruction en Pologne
france24fr.description: Volodymyr Zelensky est absent de la conférence sur la reconstruction de l’Ukraine à Gdańsk, sur fond de tensions croissantes avec la présidence polonaise. Un différend historique autour de l’Armée insurrectionnelle ukrainienne ravive les crispations, malgré le soutien de longue date de la Pologne à Kyiv.

france24fr.title: Pourquoi l'Europe est-elle si exposée aux dômes de chaleur ?
france24fr.description: De l'Espagne à l'Allemagne, en passant par le Royaume-Uni et l'Italie, tous nos voisins sont confrontés à cette vague de chaleur exceptionnelle. Pourquoi l'Europe est-elle particulièrement exposée ? Pourquoi notre continent se réchauffe-t-il deux fois plus vite que le reste du monde ?

france24fr.title: Deux puissants séismes frappent le Venezuela et provoquent des dégâts considérables
france24fr.description: Deux séismes de magnitude 7,2 puis 7,5, survenus à quelques secondes d’intervalle, ont provoqué d’importants dégâts au Venezuela, notamment à Caracas, où plusieurs bâtiments se sont effondrés. Face à un bilan provisoire de dizaines de morts et de centaines de blessés, les autorités ont décrété l’état d’urgence tandis que les États-Unis ont proposé leur aide.

france24fr.title: Cristiano Ronaldo, premier joueur à marquer dans six Coupes du monde
france24fr.description:
#Mondial2026 : CR7 entre un peu plus dans la légende 🇵🇹 
 
Grâce à la victoire du Portugal 5-0 face à l’Ouzbékistan, Cristiano Ronaldo devient le premier joueur à marquer lors de six Coupes du monde consécutives. 
 
Avec 10 buts, il est aussi désormais le meilleur buteur portugais de l’histoire du Mondial.

france24fr.title: À Paris, les Champs Élysées n'échappent pas à la canicule
france24fr.description: Les Champs-Élysées, la plus belle avenue du monde, sont eux aussi frappés par les très fortes chaleurs qui touchent l'ensemble de la France. phys-org.title: Scientists target soybean cyst nematode by cutting off its food supply
phys-org.description: Agricultural scientists are rethinking their battle plans against plant parasites that cause billions of dollars in annual yield losses for American farmers.

phys-org.title: Quantum waves reveal one-sided motion marking elusive critical states
phys-org.description: Sound waves, light waves and other types of waves, generally spread freely through space and over time. In 1958, physicist Philip W. Anderson first described a phenomenon via which irregularities or other sources of disorder in materials would prevent waves from propagating freely, which is now known as Anderson localization.

phys-org.title: Self-propelled actin filaments may explain how cells change shape spontaneously
phys-org.description: Cells can spontaneously change shape even without external signals, but the underlying mechanisms behind this form of self-organization have remained unclear. Now, researchers from Japan have discovered self-propelled treadmilling actin filaments (SpTAs), mobile protein assemblies that function as self-propelled particles. The team's work shows that even though SpTAs move randomly, they push the cell membrane outward to grow protrusions, thereby defining the overall shape of the cell. The w

phys-org.title: Space shuttle ready for new mission in California
phys-org.description: The space shuttle Endeavour, which took astronauts into orbit 25 times, went on display at the California Science Center on its final mission Wednesday.

phys-org.title: Australia's under-16 social media ban shows little early effect on teen use: Research
phys-org.description: Australia's social media ban for under-16s has had little impact on teenagers' scrolling habits, researchers said Thursday in one of the first evaluations of the world-leading measures.

phys-org.title: Secret cameras, mics and AI reveal rare Cambodia wildlife
phys-org.description: Above the patter of rain cascading through the jungle canopy comes the haunting call of a pileated gibbon singing to fend off intruders in Cambodia's Cardamom Mountains.

phys-org.title: Shorter front-leg strides can be an early warning sign of dementia in senior dogs
phys-org.description: Scientists have shown that the stride length of the front legs (but not the hind legs) of senior and geriatric dogs decreases as their cognitive performance worsens. In contrast, chronological age itself was a poor predictor of stride length. A similar reduction in step length has been well documented in people with dementia. These results suggest that a decline in stride length could be an early warning sign of canine dementia, and so an informative new tool for veterinarians.

phys-org.title: Precious drops: Spray helps crop farmers facing declining rainfall
phys-org.description: A spray made from a biodegradable polymer capable of capturing and redirecting water to crop seeds could be the key to drought-proofing Western Australian farms.

phys-org.title: Designer proteins unlock near-infrared and SWIR glow for deeper tissue imaging
phys-org.description: Researchers at the National Center for Tumor Diseases (NCT/UCC) in Dresden, including Oliver Bruns and Dr. Bernardo Arús, are participating in an international study that has, for the first time, developed novel proteins for near-infrared (NIR) and short-wave infrared imaging (SWIR). The research was conducted in collaboration with an international team that included chemistry Nobel laureate David Baker, who was honored in 2024 for his work on computational protein design. The study, with shared

phys-org.title: Ancient stories inform modern understanding of volcanic eruptions
phys-org.description: A new international study has found that Indigenous oral traditions, some thousands of years old, hold valuable and often overlooked insights into volcanic eruptions—offering important lessons for modern disaster preparedness. phys-org.title: 'Fingerprints' of black hole's event horizon detected for first time
phys-org.description: Scientists have detected the "fingerprints" of a black hole's event horizon—the boundary from which nothing can escape—for the first time, according to research published Wednesday.

phys-org.title: 'Super-puff' planets less dense than cotton candy discovered by international team
phys-org.description: An international collaboration has discovered two of the lowest-density giant planets ever detected: rare "super-puff" planets with densities lower than candy floss. The study—led by the University of Oxford, in collaboration with Université Côte d'Azur/Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur and the University of Birmingham—has been published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

phys-org.title: Pesticide widespread in blood of French Indies adults: Study
phys-org.description: Eight in 10 adults in the French West Indies have a toxic pesticide in their blood decades after banana growers stopped using it, a study said Wednesday.

phys-org.title: Did gravitational tides cause Earth's extinctions?
phys-org.description: Life on Earth took a long evolutionary journey that eventually created us, the purportedly intelligent species that dominates the planet. But there was no grand plan or design, only happenstance, nature and luck. Life on Earth suffered multiple extinctions, but got up, dusted itself off and continued on its long march to complexity.

phys-org.title: Laser experiments push helium to record shock pressures
phys-org.description: Deep inside gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn, hydrogen and helium coexist under pressures millions of times greater than Earth's atmosphere. Under those conditions, helium may separate from hydrogen and influence a planet's internal heat flow, structure and magnetic field. Understanding these processes and how these materials behave under extreme conditions is essential to building accurate models of planetary evolution.

phys-org.title: How longer exciton lifetimes could ease efficiency trade-off in organic solar cells
phys-org.description: Although the efficiency of organic solar cells has now risen to more than 20%, there are physical limits that make it difficult to further increase their performance. A research team from Linköping University in Sweden, the University of Potsdam, the Paul-Drude-Institut in Berlin and other collaborators has now demonstrated which physical processes limit a key parameter in the performance of organic solar cells. This opens up the possibility of overcoming the long-standing efficiency limits of o

phys-org.title: Mathematical modeling helps advance use of magnetic particles in targeted drug-delivery systems
phys-org.description: A Florida State University computational scientist is paving the way for future medical breakthroughs by developing mathematical models and simulations to predict the behavior of a unique drug-delivery method, which aims to deploy treatments directly to targeted sites in the body.

phys-org.title: Drifting tuna gear creates risks for wildlife in protected marine areas
phys-org.description: An international study co-authored by a University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa researcher has found that drifting devices used by the global tuna fishing industry are entering marine protected areas around the world, creating potential risks for wildlife and sensitive ocean habitats.

undark.title: Advocacy Groups Express Mixed Views on Embryo Editing
undark.description: At least two new start-up companies, Preventive and Origin Genomics, say they are developing strategies that combine gene editing with in vitro fertilization to correct disease-causing mutations. Advocacy groups for people living with these genetic disorders have been quiet on the developments.

undark.title: Interview: California Lawmaker Calls for a Peptide Working Group
undark.description: Amid a national push to ease restrictions on certain peptides, California legislator Joe Patterson has introduced a state-level bill that would to establish a working group tasked with making recommendations to allow physicians and hospitals, among others, to prescribe and study promising peptides.

undark.title: Making Sense of Data From Wearable Health Trackers
undark.description: Wearable health devices such as smartwatches, glucose monitors, and sleep trackers are blurring the line between consumer wellness and clinical medicine. One physician argues that validation standards and privacy protections must be established to ensure the usefulness of the data these devices generate.

undark.title: In California, a Plan to Help Wildlife Cross a Busy Freeway
undark.description: The 101 freeway in California bisects a mountainous region where threatened cougars and other animals are blocked without a viable path across 10 lanes of heavily trafficked roadway. But an ambitious 210-foot “vegetated bridge” will soon be home to what organizers say is the largest wildlife crossing anywhere in the world.

undark.title: Promising ‘Liquid Biopsies’ May Not Be Ready for Primetime
undark.description: Multi-cancer early detection tests seek to spot cancer from a single blood draw. Enabling earlier cancer diagnoses could help save lives and limit the need for invasive interventions. But while the tests are promising, physicians have expressed doubt about routine use by low-risk and asymptomatic individuals.

undark.title: Book Review: How Radio Astronomy Made the Invisible Visible
undark.description: According to astronomer Emma Chapman’s revelatory “The Echoing Universe,” the history of radio astronomy is filled with surprises that have revealed parts of the universe that would otherwise remain hidden and invisible — DIY instruments, secrets accidentally uncovered, and persistent connections to Earth.

undark.title: Risk Aversion in Science Stifles Innovation
undark.description: Does the scientific enterprise play it too safe? C. Brandon Ogbunu argues that risk-taking in science involves a willingness to reflect on the processes and incentives of the profession — and to dramatically overhaul them if they do not work. Only then can true scientific innovation take shape.

undark.title: A Peptide, a Secretive Scientist, and a Debate Over Evidence
undark.description: Access to unapproved peptides like BPC-157 has become a cause célèbre for the MAHA movement. Undark contributing editor Sara Talpos digs into the untold history of BPC-157 and its long journey from the scientific margins to the center of a debate over U.S. drug regulation.

undark.title: Book Review: Within Our Cells, the Miracle of Constant Mutation
undark.description: Our cells are constantly mutating in a battle for the survival of the fittest that is raging inside us daily, Roxanne Khamsi writes in “Beyond Inheritance.” Many of these mutations are harmless, others are cellular deviants that lead to disease, and remarkably, some can actually self-correct.

undark.title: The Six-Week Postpartum Checkup Comes Too Late
undark.description: In the U.S., maternity care generally ends with a checkup scheduled six weeks after giving birth. This single doctor’s appointment may be efficient for billing and discharge protocols, but the timing reflects the structure of the health care system more than the reality of maternal recovery.

proj-syn.title: Who Gains in an AI-Supercharged Economy?
proj-syn.description: If AI delivers as promised and fundamentally transforms the economy, we will have moved from the current investment phase, where AI builders dominate, to one where AI users will reap the greatest reward. That is what happens every time an innovation becomes a general-purpose technology.

proj-syn.title: Development in a Time of Disruption
proj-syn.description: Once firms and economies ascend to market dominance, they often kick away the ladder behind them and erect barriers to market entry to stymie would-be challengers. But developing countries can and do leapfrog incumbent technologies, and conditions for doing so may be particularly favorable now.

proj-syn.title: Trump’s Un-American Capitalism
proj-syn.description: The current US administration's openly corrupt style of crony capitalism is the antithesis of the institutional foundation on which the US economy was built. The winners in the new oligarchic competition are not those who make the best products, but rather those who are best at flattering the mad king.

proj-syn.title: Can the Manchester Model Save Britain?
proj-syn.description: Following a decades-long effort to lay the foundations for economic dynamism, Greater Manchester has become the UK’s fastest-growing region. While the Manchester model cannot be precisely replicated at the national level, it does carry important lessons for outgoing Prime Minister Keir Starmer's likely successor.

proj-syn.title: How Trillionaires Are Really Made
proj-syn.description: Some may argue that the world’s first trillionaire is a story of technological triumph and a win for American capitalism. But markets have not bet on cutting-edge technology or a company too big to fail, but rather on the idea of a mega-monopolist with wealth and influence so vast that the US government will not allow him to fail.

proj-syn.title: Cities Show How Climate Action Makes Life Better
proj-syn.description: Cities have shown that a combination of adaptation measures and energy efficiency can save lives, improve well-being, reduce energy costs, and create conditions for sustainable growth. A new partnership seeks to help mayors and city leaders scale up these efforts through technical and financial assistance.

proj-syn.title: The Myth of Global Chaos
proj-syn.description: Today’s seemingly nonstop international tumult is not as unintelligible as it seems. What pundits lazily describe as chaos is the culmination of developments that were long in the making and arrived at a time when the international system was no longer able to prevent or mitigate geopolitical shocks.

proj-syn.title: The Microfinance Debate Is Missing the Point
proj-syn.description: For too long, policymakers, economists, and investors have focused on whether microfinance actually helps people, reducing a complex issue to a meaningless yes-or-no verdict. The most important questions concern how loans are designed, delivered, and regulated, who receives them, and what they are used for.

proj-syn.title: Turning Latin America’s Resilience Into Growth
proj-syn.description: Economic stabilization has been a significant achievement for Latin America and the Caribbean, a region with a long history of financial crises. But these countries need a well-sequenced reform agenda to attract private investment and create the growth engine that will translate hard-won gains into higher living standards.

proj-syn.title: The World Cup vs. the Extremists
proj-syn.description: Germany’s 2026 World Cup team, like so many others in the tournament, shows that loving one’s country and welcoming newcomers are not incompatible impulses. Although activists on the far left and the far right would have us believe otherwise, most ordinary people implicitly recognize this.

proj-syn.title: Beyond Brexit—and Back to Europe
proj-syn.description: Those who follow only intergovernmental negotiations or debates in the media might think that nothing has changed in the decade since the United Kingdom's voters decided to leave the European Union. Yet new polling finds that large majorities on both sides of the English Channel now support re-engagement.

proj-syn.title: Trump’s March of Folly in Iran
proj-syn.description: In promoting his “deal” with Iran, US President Donald Trump has tried to dress up a humiliating defeat as a victory. While it’s tempting to blame this outcome on incompetent leadership, it stems more from the policies and institutions that have allowed entertainers and profiteers to rise to power.

proj-syn.title: Alan Greenspan’s Mixed Legacy
proj-syn.description: The longtime Federal Reserve chair inferred from past crises that lightly regulated markets, while prone to excesses, could right themselves sufficiently to avoid imperiling the financial system and the economy. The correct lesson would have been that markets require strict regulation, and that competent technocrats are essential.

proj-syn.title: Will AI Yield Abundance Without Purpose?
proj-syn.description: Work and employment play a uniquely powerful role in structuring people’s days and conferring a sense of belonging, status, and self-worth. Although AI boosters insist that people would organically find new sources of meaning if most jobs are automated, there is no reason to assume so.

proj-syn.title: To Avoid Climate Peril, the World Must Electrify
proj-syn.description: The war in the Gulf has unleashed powerful market forces that the rest of the world can harness to accelerate electrification and keep the Paris climate agreement's primary objectives on track. Doing so will not only mitigate climate change, but also strengthen economic resilience worldwide.

proj-syn.title: What the Iran War Taught the World About Food Security
proj-syn.description: Perhaps the most unsettling lesson from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is the gap between what we knew and how we prepared. Countries should use whatever easing of immediate pressures occurs to strengthen resilience before the next shock arrives.

proj-syn.title: The Orange Bandit
proj-syn.description: According to the Roman Emperor Tiberius, a ruler can either “shear the sheep” for many years, by encouraging productive activity from which to generate tax revenues, or he can “skin them alive” just once. By brazenly using the US government to pillage the country, President Donald Trump has apparently chosen the knife.

proj-syn.title: How (Not) to Conserve Tropical Forests
proj-syn.description: Although the Tropical Forest Forever Facility that emerged from the last United Nations Climate Conference is unlikely to succeed, critically important global conservation efforts are not doomed. Through sustainability-linked sovereign bonds and loans, tropical countries can overcome the TFFF’s fatal flaws.
